eli5: The P/E ratio tells you how much investors are willing to pay for every dollar a company earns. If a company earns $1 and its stock costs $20, the P/E ratio is 20 — meaning people are paying $20 for each $1 of profit.
analogy: It's like paying $20 for a lemonade stand that makes $1 per day — you're betting it'll keep growing.

eli5: Beta measures how much a stock moves compared to the overall market. A beta of 2 means if the market goes up 1%, the stock tends to go up 2% — but also falls twice as hard.
analogy: Think of beta like a volume knob — a high-beta stock turns market moves way up, while a low-beta stock keeps things quiet.

eli5: The expense ratio is the annual fee a fund charges you, expressed as a percentage of your investment. A 1% expense ratio means for every $1,000 you invest, the fund takes $10 per year to cover its costs.
analogy: It's like a management fee your landlord charges for running an apartment complex — it comes out of your returns automatically.

eli5: Market cap is the total value of a company's stock — calculated by multiplying the share price by the total number of shares. It tells you the size of the company in the eyes of investors.
analogy: If every share of Apple is a piece of a pie and each slice costs $170, market cap is the total price of the whole pie.

eli5: Volatility measures how wildly a stock's price swings up and down over time. High volatility means big, unpredictable price jumps; low volatility means the price moves slowly and steadily.
analogy: A roller coaster has high volatility — a long flat highway road trip has low volatility.

eli5: A drawdown is how much an investment has fallen from its peak value before recovering. If your portfolio hit $10,000 then dropped to $7,000, that's a 30% drawdown.
analogy: Imagine hiking to the top of a hill, then sliding partway down before climbing back up — the slide is the drawdown.

eli5: An ETF is a basket of many stocks or bonds bundled together that you can buy and sell on the stock market like a single share. Instead of buying Apple, Microsoft, and Google separately, you can buy one ETF that owns all of them.
analogy: It's like buying a sampler platter at a restaurant — you get a little bit of everything instead of committing to just one dish.

eli5: Yield is the income you earn from an investment, shown as a percentage of what you paid. A 5% yield on a $1,000 bond means you receive $50 per year in interest.
analogy: Yield is like the interest rate on a savings account — it tells you how much your money is paying you just to sit there.

eli5: Liquidity describes how quickly and easily you can turn an investment into cash without losing much value. Cash is perfectly liquid; a house is very illiquid because it takes months to sell.
analogy: Water is liquid — it pours instantly. Ice (illiquid) takes time and heat to turn back into something you can use.

eli5: Diversification means spreading your money across many different investments so that if one fails, it doesn't wipe you out. It's the investing version of not putting all your eggs in one basket.
analogy: If you own 10 lemonade stands in different neighborhoods, one bad rainstorm can't ruin your whole business.
keywords: don't put all eggs in one basket

eli5: A bull market is a period when stock prices are rising and investors feel optimistic about the economy. It's generally defined as a 20% or more rise from a recent low.
analogy: A bull charges forward with energy — a bull market is the stock market charging upward with momentum.

eli5: A bear market is when stock prices fall 20% or more from their recent peak and investors are pessimistic. It can last months or even years before prices recover.
analogy: A bear swipes downward with its paw — a bear market is the stock market swiping prices down.

eli5: An index fund automatically copies a market index like the S&P 500, buying every stock in that index. Instead of a manager picking stocks, the fund just follows the index passively, keeping costs very low.
analogy: It's like a copycat student who copies the top student's answers — the index fund just copies the market's homework.

eli5: A dividend is a portion of a company's profits paid out directly to shareholders, usually every quarter. If you own 100 shares of a company that pays a $0.50 dividend, you receive $50 just for owning the stock.
analogy: It's like being a partial owner of a pizza shop and getting a check in the mail every time the shop makes good money.

eli5: The spread is the difference between the price buyers are willing to pay (bid) and the price sellers are asking for (ask). A wider spread means higher trading costs; a narrow spread means the market is very efficient.
analogy: It's like a currency exchange booth at an airport — they buy your dollars at a low price and sell at a higher one, keeping the difference.

eli5: Short selling is when you borrow shares, sell them hoping the price drops, then buy them back cheaper and return them — keeping the difference as profit. It's a way to bet that a stock will go down.
analogy: Imagine borrowing your friend's old iPhone 12, selling it for $400 today, then buying it back for $300 when newer models come out and pocketing the $100 difference.

eli5: A hedge is an investment made specifically to reduce the risk of another investment going wrong. It's like insurance — you pay a small cost now to protect yourself from a bigger loss later.
analogy: Buying an umbrella before you go on a picnic is a hedge against rain ruining your day.

eli5: Your portfolio is the collection of all the investments you own — stocks, bonds, ETFs, crypto, and anything else. Think of it as your personal investment team roster.
analogy: A portfolio is like your music playlist — it's the combination of all your favorite songs (investments) that you've chosen together.

eli5: Asset allocation is how you divide your money among different types of investments like stocks, bonds, and cash. It's one of the most important decisions you can make because it determines your overall risk level.
analogy: It's like deciding how to split a meal — 60% main course (stocks), 30% side dish (bonds), 10% dessert (alternatives).

eli5: Rebalancing is when you adjust your portfolio back to your original plan after prices shift it off course. If stocks grew so much they now make up 80% of your portfolio instead of the planned 60%, you sell some stocks and buy more bonds to get back to 60/40.
analogy: It's like trimming overgrown plants in a garden — you cut back what's gotten too big to keep the whole garden balanced.

eli5: Dollar-cost averaging means investing a fixed amount of money at regular intervals, regardless of the price. This way you automatically buy more shares when prices are low and fewer when prices are high.
analogy: It's like filling up your gas tank every Monday no matter the price — sometimes you get a great deal, sometimes not, but it evens out over time.

eli5: Compound interest means you earn interest on both your original money AND on the interest you've already earned. Over time, this creates a snowball effect where your money grows faster and faster.
analogy: It's like a snowball rolling down a hill — it picks up more snow as it goes, getting bigger and bigger the longer it rolls.

eli5: Risk tolerance is how much loss or uncertainty you can handle emotionally and financially without panic-selling your investments. Someone with high risk tolerance can watch their portfolio drop 40% and stay calm; low risk tolerance means losses keep them up at night.
analogy: It's like choosing a roller coaster at an amusement park — some people love the biggest, scariest drop, others prefer the gentle family ride.

eli5: A stock split is when a company divides its existing shares into more shares, making each share cheaper. If Apple does a 4-for-1 split, every one $400 share becomes four $100 shares — you own more shares but the total value stays the same.
analogy: It's like cutting a pizza into 8 slices instead of 4 — more slices, but the same amount of pizza overall.

eli5: An IPO is when a private company sells shares to the public for the very first time on a stock exchange. It's how companies raise money from everyday investors and how you first get the chance to buy a piece of a company like that.
analogy: An IPO is like a restaurant opening its doors to the public for the first time — previously only insiders could eat there, now anyone can walk in.

eli5: EPS tells you how much profit a company made for each share of stock outstanding. If a company earned $1 billion and has 500 million shares, the EPS is $2 — meaning each share represents $2 of profit.
analogy: If a class sells 100 cookies for $200 total profit, each cookie's 'EPS' is $2 — it's each cookie's share of the profit.

eli5: ROE shows how good a company is at turning shareholders' money into profit. A 20% ROE means for every $100 investors put in, the company generates $20 of profit — higher is generally better.
analogy: It's like knowing how good a baker is at turning flour and ingredients (equity) into delicious profit-making cakes.

eli5: The debt-to-equity ratio compares how much debt a company has versus how much equity (shareholder money) it uses. A ratio of 2 means the company borrowed $2 for every $1 of equity — higher ratios mean more financial risk.
analogy: It's like buying a house with 80% mortgage and 20% down payment — you're heavily leveraged, which is riskier but lets you buy more.

eli5: The price-to-book ratio compares what investors pay for a stock to the actual accounting value of the company's assets. A P/B of 3 means you're paying $3 for every $1 of assets the company actually owns.
analogy: It's like paying $30,000 for a used car that the book says is worth $10,000 — you're betting the car's brand and reputation make it worth more.

eli5: A moving average smooths out a stock's price history by averaging prices over a set period, like the last 50 or 200 days. It helps you see the overall trend by filtering out daily noise and wild swings.
analogy: It's like averaging your grades over a semester instead of just looking at one test score — you see the real trend, not just a bad day.

eli5: A support level is a price where a stock has repeatedly stopped falling and bounced back up. Traders watch these levels because they suggest buyers tend to step in around that price to prevent further declines.
analogy: It's like a trampoline at the bottom — every time the ball hits that level, it bounces back up.

eli5: A resistance level is a price where a stock has repeatedly struggled to rise above. It's like a ceiling — sellers tend to show up in force at that price, pushing the price back down each time it tries to break through.
analogy: Imagine trying to push a bowling ball up a steep hill to a specific mark — it keeps rolling back down at that same spot every time.

eli5: Volume is the number of shares of a stock traded during a given period. High volume means lots of people are buying or selling, which usually means stronger conviction behind a price move.
analogy: Volume is like the crowd noise at a concert — the louder (higher) the crowd, the more people are paying attention and participating.

eli5: A market order is an instruction to buy or sell a stock immediately at whatever the current price is. You trade instantly but might not get the exact price you saw on screen because prices move constantly.
analogy: A market order is like walking up to a street food cart and saying 'I'll take whatever you're selling at whatever price' — fast, but no price guarantee.

eli5: A limit order lets you set the maximum price you'll pay to buy or the minimum price you'll accept to sell. Your order only executes if the market hits your specified price.
analogy: It's like telling a used car dealer 'I'll only buy this car if you can get the price down to $15,000 — not a penny more.'

eli5: A stop-loss order automatically sells your stock if the price falls to a level you set, limiting your losses. It's like a safety net that kicks in before your losses get too big.
analogy: It's like setting an alarm that automatically turns off the stove if the temperature gets too high — protecting you from a bigger disaster.

eli5: Trading on margin means borrowing money from your broker to buy more investments than you could afford with your own cash alone. It amplifies gains — but also losses, and you pay interest on what you borrow.
analogy: It's like using a credit card to buy stocks — you can buy more, but if prices fall you still owe the full borrowed amount plus interest.

eli5: Options are contracts that give you the right (but not the obligation) to buy or sell a stock at a specific price by a certain date. They can be used to protect investments or to speculate on price moves with less money upfront.
analogy: An option is like a coupon that says 'you can buy this TV for $500 anytime in the next 30 days' — you don't have to use it, but you have the right to.

eli5: Futures are contracts to buy or sell something at a specific price on a specific future date, and unlike options, you are obligated to complete the trade. They're used by farmers, airlines, and investors to lock in prices and manage risk.
analogy: A futures contract is like a farmer agreeing today to sell 1,000 bushels of wheat in December at $6 per bushel — locking in the price regardless of what happens.

eli5: Inflation is the gradual increase in prices over time, which means your money buys less than it used to. If inflation is 3% per year, something that costs $100 today will cost $103 next year.
analogy: Inflation is like a slow hole in your wallet — every year, a little bit of your money's buying power leaks out if you don't invest it.

eli5: A Systematic Investment Plan (SIP) is a disciplined way to invest a fixed amount of money regularly (e.g., monthly) into mutual funds or stocks, rather than investing a huge lump sum all at once.
analogy: Like a gym routine for your savings — instead of trying to bench-press 300 lbs on day one, you build financial muscle bit by bit every single month.

eli5: A mutual fund pools together money from thousands of everyday investors to buy a professionally managed bundle of stocks, bonds, and other assets.
analogy: A potluck dinner — instead of cooking a 10-course banquet by yourself, everyone contributes, and everybody enjoys a diverse, hearty feast.

eli5: Net Asset Value (NAV) is the market value of one unit of a mutual fund or ETF, calculated daily by subtracting total liabilities from total assets and dividing by outstanding units.
analogy: Counting all the cash in a piggy bank and dividing it by the number of coins inside to find the exact value of each coin slice.

eli5: Return on Investment (ROI) measures how much money you gained or lost relative to what you originally invested, expressed as a percentage.
analogy: Planting 1 apple seed and harvesting 5 juicy apples from the tree — those extra 4 apples represent your return on the seed.

eli5: FOMO is the psychological urge to buy a skyrocketing asset because you see others boasting about massive profits and dread being left behind.
analogy: Seeing a huge crowd run screaming into a store and joining the stampede without knowing what is even on sale.

eli5: HODL is investor slang for refusing to sell your assets during sharp market crashes, committing to hold them long-term through thick and thin.
analogy: Staying securely strapped into your rollercoaster seat during a vertical drop rather than trying to jump off mid-loop.

eli5: A stop-loss is an automated order placed with your broker to sell an investment if its price drops to a predetermined level, capping your maximum loss.
analogy: An emergency brake on a runaway train — if the train starts rolling backward down a cliff, the brakes lock before you crash.

eli5: Annual Percentage Yield (APY) is the real yearly rate of return earned on an investment or savings account, factoring in the boost from compounding interest.
analogy: The true speed reading of how quickly your bank balance naturally multiplies over a full 12-month calendar year.

eli5: Support is a price floor where a declining stock tends to stop dropping and bounce back up, because eager buyers step in to purchase at that attractive price.
analogy: Like a trampoline beneath a bouncing ball — every time the ball drops down and hits the trampoline, it gets propelled back upward.

eli5: Resistance is a price ceiling where an advancing stock struggles to climb higher, because sellers rush in to lock in profits, creating heavy downward selling pressure.
analogy: Like a glass ceiling in an attic — you can jump as hard as you want, but your head knocks against the barrier until momentum breaks through.

eli5: An Area of Interest (AOI) is a critical price zone on a chart where historical trading activity, support, or resistance suggests major buying or selling will take place.
analogy: Like a busy highway toll booth or airport terminal — you know that is where all the traffic converges and key action will happen.

eli5: Technical analysis is the practice of evaluating investments by studying past market statistics, price movements, and chart patterns rather than business balance sheets.
analogy: Studying the flight radar and weather patterns of an airplane to predict its landing time rather than inspecting the airline's corporate headquarters.

eli5: Capital gains are the profit you make when you sell an investment for more than you paid for it. If you bought a stock at $50 and sold it at $80, your capital gain is $30.
analogy: It's like buying a concert ticket for $100 and selling it for $200 when the show sells out — the $100 profit is your capital gain.

eli5: Blue chip stocks are shares of large, well-established, financially stable companies with a long track record of reliable performance. Think Apple, Microsoft, or Johnson & Johnson.
analogy: Blue chip stocks are like the star players on a sports team — they have a proven track record and are the safest bets on the roster.

eli5: Penny stocks are shares of very small companies that trade at low prices, usually under $5 per share. They're extremely risky and volatile — many people lose money chasing quick profits.
analogy: Penny stocks are like scratch-off lottery tickets — cheap to buy, but the odds of striking it rich are very low.

eli5: A bond is a loan you give to a company or government, and they pay you back with interest over time. Bonds are generally safer than stocks but offer lower returns.
analogy: Buying a bond is like lending money to a friend who promises to pay you back with extra interest after a set period.

eli5: Fundamental analysis is evaluating a stock by studying the company's financial health — revenue, profits, debt, and growth potential — rather than just looking at the price chart.
analogy: It's like checking a restaurant's health inspection score, reviews, and menu quality before deciding to eat there, rather than just judging by how long the line is.

eli5: The 52-week high is the highest price a stock has reached in the past year, and the 52-week low is the lowest. They help you see where the stock is trading relative to its recent range.
analogy: It's like looking at your fitness tracker's highest and lowest heart rates over the past year to see where you stand today.

eli5: Earnings season is the period each quarter when most publicly traded companies report their financial results. Stock prices often move sharply during this time based on whether results beat or miss expectations.
analogy: It's like report card day at school — every company shows its grades, and the market reacts to who passed and who failed.

eli5: Market sentiment is the overall mood or attitude of investors toward the market or a particular asset — whether they feel optimistic (bullish) or pessimistic (bearish).
analogy: It's like the vibe at a party — if everyone is excited and dancing, the sentiment is positive. If people are leaving early and looking bored, sentiment is negative.

eli5: A dead cat bounce is a brief, temporary recovery in a stock's price during a long downtrend. The price bounces up slightly but then continues falling — it's not a real recovery.
analogy: Even a dead cat will bounce if dropped from high enough — the small bounce doesn't mean the cat is alive again.

eli5: An all-time high is the highest price a stock or asset has ever reached in its entire trading history. Reaching an ATH means the asset has never been more valuable.
analogy: It's like breaking a world record in the Olympics — the athlete has never performed better than this moment.

eli5: DRIP automatically uses the cash dividends you earn to buy more shares of the same stock, instead of taking the cash. This lets your investment grow faster through compounding.
analogy: It's like a fruit tree that drops seeds — instead of eating the seeds, you plant them to grow more trees, which drop more seeds, and so on.

eli5: A sector is a group of companies that operate in the same area of the economy, like technology, healthcare, or energy. Sectors help you categorize and compare similar businesses.
analogy: It's like sorting animals at a zoo — all the fish go in the aquarium, all the reptiles go in the reptile house. Sectors group similar companies together.

eli5: RSI is a momentum indicator that measures whether a stock is being bought too much (overbought, above 70) or sold too much (oversold, below 30). It ranges from 0 to 100.
analogy: RSI is like a thermostat for stock buying — if it reads too hot (above 70), the stock might cool down. If it reads too cold (below 30), it might warm up.

eli5: MACD (Moving Average Convergence Divergence) is a trend-following momentum indicator that shows the relationship between two moving averages of a stock's price. It helps identify buy and sell signals.
analogy: MACD is like watching two runners on a track — when the faster runner crosses ahead of the slower one, it signals a change in who's leading the race.

eli5: Growth stocks are expected to grow earnings fast and reinvest profits, while value stocks appear underpriced relative to their actual worth. Growth stocks are riskier but can deliver bigger gains; value stocks are steadier.
analogy: A growth stock is like a promising startup restaurant expanding rapidly; a value stock is like a solid family diner that's been around for decades but is currently having a slow month.

eli5: Large cap companies are worth over $10 billion (like Apple or Amazon), while small cap companies are worth under $2 billion. Large caps are more stable; small caps have more growth potential but higher risk.
analogy: Large cap is like a massive cruise ship — steady and hard to tip over. Small cap is like a speedboat — faster and more agile, but easier to capsize in rough waters.

eli5: Net worth is the total value of everything you own (assets) minus everything you owe (debts). It's the simplest measure of your overall financial health.
analogy: It's like your personal balance sheet — if you have $10,000 in savings and owe $3,000 on a credit card, your net worth is $7,000.

eli5: A market maker is a firm that stands ready to buy and sell stocks at any time, providing liquidity so you can always find someone to trade with. They make money from the bid-ask spread.
analogy: A market maker is like a currency exchange booth at an airport — they always have cash ready to exchange, and they make a small profit on each transaction.

eli5: A circuit breaker is a automatic trading halt triggered when the market drops too fast in a single day. It pauses trading for a set time to let investors calm down and prevent panic selling.
analogy: It's like a fire alarm in a building — when things get too hot (volatile), the alarm goes off and everyone has to step outside for a break before coming back in.

eli5: A dividend aristocrat is a company in the S&P 500 that has increased its dividend payout for at least 25 consecutive years. They are known for reliability and steady income.
analogy: A dividend aristocrat is like a reliable friend who always shows up to your birthday party, year after year, without fail — dependable and consistent.

eli5: The yield curve is a graph showing interest rates on bonds of different maturities. A normal curve slopes upward (long-term rates higher than short-term). An inverted curve (short-term higher) often predicts a recession.
analogy: The yield curve is like a weather forecast for the economy — when it looks normal, things are calm. When it flips upside down (inverted), storm clouds may be gathering.

eli5: EPS tells you how much profit a company made for each share of stock. If a company earned $1 billion with 500 million shares, the EPS is $2 per share.
analogy: If a pizza is cut into 8 slices and the whole pizza costs $24, each slice's share of the cost is $3 — EPS is like each slice's share of the profit.

eli5: The P/E ratio shows how much investors pay for every $1 of a company's earnings. A P/E of 25 means investors pay $25 for each $1 of profit the company makes.
analogy: It's like paying $25 for a lemonade stand that earns $1 per day — you're paying a premium because you expect it to grow.
